question: How can a movement this short and fast still hold a sonata’s whole argument?
intro: A two-minute storm in E minor, played at scherzo speed and built in blocks of four bars, still carries a sonata’s whole argument: two related themes, a central passage that works the opening bass and sinks to a hush, and a return that comes as a release.

sections.label: Exposition · E minor, then B minor
Development · the opening bass, then a hush
Recapitulation · E minor
sections.mNote: the opening returns after the quietest point

cues.title: A sonata in blocks of four
cues.text: Marked Prestissimo, ff and ben marcato, the movement opens in E minor in 6/8 and is often played straight after the Vivace. Biamonti hears a sonata form of two expressively related themes, development, recapitulation and conclusion, built from symmetrical blocks of four bars.
cues.evidence: The tempo and dynamic markings and the 6/8 metre are on printed p. 101 of the Breitkopf score (IMSLP #51804). Biamonti’s description is quoted at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/Opus109/; Wikipedia’s Op. 109 article describes the two movements as linked. The report’s first window is −15.4 dB with 2.4 attacks per second; no bar is timed.

cues.title: Towards B minor
cues.text: From about 0:20 the harmony settles in B minor, the key of the second theme. Its material is closely related to the first: Brendel, cited by Wikipedia, finds the usual contrast of subjects absent here, so the change of key does much of the contrasting.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 0:20 (novelty 0.62) is followed by local-key estimates of B minor from 0:20 to 0:40 (r 0.73–0.84) and B major at 0:45 (r 0.82), with F♯ and C♯ prominent. The relation of the themes is from Biamonti (https://www.lvbeethoven.org/Opus109/) and Brendel as cited in Wikipedia; bars are not aligned.

cues.title: A dedication, a flawed first edition
cues.text: Beethoven dedicated the sonata to Maximiliane Brentano, the musically gifted daughter of his friends Franz and Antonie Brentano. Schlesinger of Berlin published it in November 1821 with many errors: Beethoven had sent his hard-to-read autograph and was too ill to proofread the prints.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Op. 109 article, genesis and publication section (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven)), citing Meredith; the dedication is also printed on the title page of the Breitkopf score (IMSLP #51804, p. 97).

cues.title: The opening bass, then a hush
cues.text: From about 0:52 the storm turns inward. In the score a long passage of repeated B in the bass lies beneath slowly falling notes, then repeated C; Larner notes that the middle section draws its material from the bass of the first theme. By 1:10 attacks nearly stop.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 0:52 (novelty 0.46) and 0:58 (0.68); level falls from −24.4 dB at 0:50 to −29.0 dB at 1:05 and −33.9 dB at 1:10 (0.2 attacks per second); the key estimate reads E minor at 0:55 and 1:05 and C major at 1:00. The repeated B and C in the bass are on printed p. 102 of the score (IMSLP #51804); Larner’s remark is in his Op. 109 note. Bars are not aligned.

cues.title: The return after the hush
cues.text: At about 1:24 the hush breaks. After the quietest music of the movement, near −40 dB at 1:15, the level jumps some 24 dB within five seconds as the opening returns in E minor. The score marks una corda and sempre più piano, then tutte le corde and ff.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:24 (novelty 1.00); level −40.3 dB at 1:15, −35.5 dB at 1:20 and −11.6 dB at 1:25, with the key estimate E minor (r 0.97) at 1:25. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed pp. 102–103) marks una corda, sempre più piano, pp with a fermata, then tutte le corde ff at the head of p. 103. Levels are relative within this recording.

cues.title: The second theme returns in E minor
cues.text: The music that sat in B minor in the exposition, about twenty seconds in, comes back now in the home key of E minor, five semitones higher. The recurrence is exact enough to hear: the same shape, a fourth up.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 23.5–44.0 s with 104.5–125.0 s at a transposition of five semitones upward (B to E; similarity 0.93). The reading of the first as second-theme material follows the sonata-form analyses cited above; the endpoint is an approximate window, not a barline.

cues.title: A quiet close, then forte chords
cues.text: One of the loudest windows falls near 2:00; then the music drops to a quiet passage and builds again. The score ends on forte staccato E minor chords. The silence by 2:15 is the last chord dying away, not a written diminuendo.
cues.evidence: Level is −23.3 dB at 1:55, −12.3 dB at 2:00, −21.1 dB at 2:05 and −14.8 dB at 2:10 (3.0 attacks per second), then −63.7 dB at 2:15, the end of the file; boundaries at 1:50 (0.42) and 2:02 (0.49). The last systems of the score (IMSLP #51804, printed p. 104) show a quiet passage, a crescendo and f staccato chords. Bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: A pedal-like bass, a thinner storm
transitions.from: Exposition · E minor, then B minor
transitions.to: Development · the opening bass, then a hush
transitions.how: The loud writing in and around B, heard from about 0:40, gives way to quieter music. In the score the bass repeats B, the dominant of E minor, across several systems while slowly falling notes move above it, and it then moves to repeated C. Larner hears the middle section taking its material from the bass of the first theme. The Prestissimo tempo does not change, but the storm thins, and the repeated B builds a foundation for the return.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 0:52 (0.46) and 0:58 (0.68); level falls from −15.1 dB at 0:45 to −24.4 dB at 0:50 and −29.0 dB at 1:05. The repeated B and C in the bass are on printed p. 102 of the score (IMSLP #51804); Larner’s remark is in his Op. 109 note. Bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: Una corda, then everything at once
transitions.from: Development · the opening bass, then a hush
transitions.how: After the repeated B and C, the lines become imitative and softer. The score marks una corda and sempre più piano, reaches pp on a fermata, and then releases tutte le corde with ff for the return of the opening in E minor. The long quiet preparation, not a loud build-up, sets up the return: the hush is the retransition, and the release at the end of it is the moment of recapitulation.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary is 1:24 (1.00); level −40.3 dB at 1:15, −35.5 dB at 1:20 and −11.6 dB at 1:25, with the key estimate E minor (r 0.97) at 1:25. The score (IMSLP #51804, printed pp. 102–103) marks una corda, sempre più piano, pp with a fermata, then tutte le corde ff at the head of p. 103. Bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: Quiet again, then a surge to the end
transitions.how: The returned second theme in E minor ends, and the movement does not slow. The score falls to a quiet passage, builds in a long crescendo, and ends on forte staccato chords in E minor. The last chord’s decay at the end of the recording is not a composed diminuendo: the written close is loud, short and clipped, which opens a sharp gap before the finale’s slow theme.
transitions.evidence: The recurrence match of the second theme ends near 125 s (an approximate window, not a barline); level −21.1 dB at 2:05 and −14.8 dB at 2:10 with 3.0 attacks per second; silence at 2:15 is the file’s end. The last systems of the score (IMSLP #51804, printed p. 104) show a quiet passage, a crescendo and f staccato chords. Bars are not aligned.

composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
